title: Gender and Adoption of Climate‐Smart Agricultural Practices in Developing Countries: Evidence From West African Countries
title_zh: 发展中国家性别与气候智慧型农业实践采纳：来自西非国家的证据
authors: Abraham Amoussouga Gero, Aklesso Y. G. Egbendewe
source: Australian Journal of Agricultural and Resource Economics
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the influence of gender on the adoption of Climate‐Smart Agriculture (CSA) practices in West Africa. An exogenous switching treatment effect regression model with the Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition method is used in the study. Data were collected from the 2018/2019 Harmonized Household Living Conditions Survey across five West African countries. The results indicate that if female plot managers had the same characteristics as their male counterparts, their likelihood of adopting CSA practices would increase, yet it would still be lower than that of men. The decomposition analysis shows a significant gender gap favouring men in Burkina Faso and Senegal, unlike in Ivory Coast and Togo. These gender differences are mainly due to structural factors such as household size, education, access to credit, commercialisation, income, livestock ownership, family labour, pesticide use, soil fertility and the availability of agricultural extension agents and cooperatives. To effectively address gender disparities in CSA adoption, policies could focus on improving these structural conditions rather than solely on ensuring equal access to production resources. This approach would enhance policy effectiveness and empower women to better utilise their agricultural resources.

title: Does the Import Invasion Explain the Mysterious Disappearance of Productivity Growth in U.S. Manufacturing?
title_zh: DP21651 进口入侵是否解释了美国制造业生产率增长的神秘消失？
authors: Robert J. Gordon, Kenneth Ryu, Robert J. Gordon; Kenneth Ryu
official: 官方在线 2026-06-21 · 来源：出版社网页
abstract: Why did U.S. manufacturing productivity stop growing after 2010? Productivity growth disappeared, evaporating from an annual rate of +3.3 percent during 1987-2010 to -0.3 percent from 2010 to 2023. This paper shifts attention from 2010 as the start of the puzzle to a decade earlier when output stopped growing. This cessation of output growth in 2000 is attributed to the invasion of imports that closed domestic plants, destroyed jobs, and squeezed profits. Then followed a chain of causation that ultimately undermined productivity growth – from falling capacity utilization, to lower investment in fixed capital and R&D, and to an erosion of innovation. Beyond the import invasion, the paper identifies a set of handicaps ranging from self-inflicted wounds to short-sighted government policy. Corporate funds were diverted from productive investment to share buybacks. Investment was distorted by environmental, health, safety, and fuel economy regulations. Other issues with government policy include a substantial reduction in public R&D and a failure to develop training programs to alleviate a decades-long shortage of skilled labor.

title: Geographic mortality differentials and the quality-quantity trade-off
title_zh: 地理死亡率差异与质量-数量权衡
authors: Sinara Gharibyan, David Gomtsyan, Èric Roca Fernández
abstract: Abstract This paper explores the relationship between geographic mortality differentials and human capital investment patterns in the Malthusian setup of 19th-century Armenia. We examine how variations in altitude are associated with mortality rates, human capital accumulation, and fertility decisions. Using detailed historical census and parish records, we document that higher-altitude areas tend to have lower population density, lower respiratory disease mortality, and lower overall mortality. Our empirical analysis also shows that individuals in these environments tend to display better numeracy skills and lower fertility rates. These findings align with the Ben-Porath hypothesis, suggesting that longer life horizons encourage shifting from child quantity to quality. Furthermore, these patterns are not driven by income differences or increased female autonomy arising from pastoral agriculture.

title: Measurement Error and Counterfactuals in Quantitative Trade and Spatial Models
title_zh: 定量贸易与空间模型中的测量误差与反事实分析
abstract: Abstract Counterfactuals in quantitative trade and spatial models are functions of the current state of the world and the model parameters. Common practice treats the current state of the world as perfectly observed, but there is good reason to believe that it is measured with error. This paper provides tools for quantifying uncertainty about counterfactuals when the current state of the world is measured with error. I recommend an empirical Bayes approach to uncertainty quantification, and show that it is both practical and theoretically justified.
